cauchy1847.short: Cauchy 1847, the method of steepest descent
cauchy1847.citation: Cauchy, A. (1847). Methode generale pour la resolution des systemes d'equations simultanees. Comptes Rendus de l'Academie des Sciences 25, 536-538.
cauchy1847.read: primary scan not read (Gallica refused access); read Lemarechal 2012, Documenta Mathematica Extra Volume ISMP, 251-254, which quotes the note (Comptes Rendus 25, 536-538, 18 October 1847)
claims: Cauchy described moving a point step by step in the direction that most decreases a function, using its partial derivatives (steepest descent), in 1847.
Cauchy outlined the method and gave no proof of convergence.
cauchy1847.does_not_prove: That the method works well on a given problem; the step size and the shape of the function decide that.

goodfellow2016.short: Goodfellow, Bengio and Courville 2016, Deep Learning
goodfellow2016.citation: Goodfellow, I., Bengio, Y., Courville, A. (2016). Deep Learning. MIT Press. Chapter 4.3 (gradient-based optimization) and chapter 8 (minibatch training).
claims: The gradient points in the direction of steepest increase; gradient descent steps in the negative gradient direction (4.3).

With a quadratic approximation, the optimal step along the steepest curvature is 1 divided by the largest Hessian eigenvalue, and a step is uphill once its second-order term outweighs its first-order term (eq. 4.9, 4.10, 8.10). The edge of 2 divided by the largest eigenvalue for a quadratic is our derivation from these, and our runs measure it.
Ill-conditioning (very different curvatures in different directions) makes gradient descent slow (8.2.1).
Training uses minibatches, so each step uses an estimate of the gradient (8.1.3).
goodfellow2016.does_not_prove: Anything about a particular trained model.

rosenbrock1960.short: Rosenbrock 1960, the curved valley test function
rosenbrock1960.citation: Rosenbrock, H. H. (1960). An automatic method for finding the greatest or least value of a function. The Computer Journal 3(3), 175-184.
rosenbrock1960.read: not read (paywalled); the function's form is from the GAMS model library entry that cites the paper; the start (-1.2, 1) is the usual one in later use, not confirmed against the paper
claims: The function f(x, y) = (1 - x)^2 + 100 (y - x^2)^2 has a long, curved, narrow valley with its minimum at (1, 1); it later became a standard hard case for gradient methods.
rosenbrock1960.does_not_prove: How hard real training problems are.

ours-surfaces.short: Night School's surfaces, computed for this film
ours-surfaces.citation: media/school/gradients/facts.json, written by tools/school/fill_gradients.mjs from system/school/gradients.mjs: exact gradients, a finite-difference check, curvatures from a finite-difference Hessian, and the stability edge found by bisection on real runs.
claims: The bowl's curvatures are 4 and 0.5; the predicted edge 2/4 = 0.5 and the measured edge agree to about 1e-13; runs at 0.5, 0.99 and 1.01 times the edge converge, crawl and diverge over 60 steps, and at 2 times the edge the loss passes the 1e12 cap at step 12; runs at 0.6 and 1.2 times the edge (the film's doubled step) converge and diverge.
Rosenbrock from (-1.2, 1) with step 0.001: loss below 1e-2 at step 3,925 and below 1e-6 at step 15,068; curvature ratio at the minimum about 2,508.
Two valleys: starts at (-0.3, 0) and (0.3, 0) end in different valleys; the right valley's bottom (0.197) is higher than the left's (-0.202).
ours-surfaces.does_not_prove: Anything about real models; these are toy surfaces chosen to show one effect each.

li2018.short: Li, Xu, Taylor, Studer and Goldstein 2018, Visualizing the Loss Landscape of Neural Nets
li2018.citation: Li, H., Xu, Z., Taylor, G., Studer, C., Goldstein, T. (2018). Visualizing the Loss Landscape of Neural Nets. NeurIPS 31. arXiv:1712.09913.
li2018.read: full text, arXiv v3 (NeurIPS 2018), sections 4, 6 and 7.1
claims: A loss surface can be viewed by plotting the loss along two random directions through the trained parameters, with each direction normalised filter by filter to the size of the weights.

In high dimensions two random directions are nearly orthogonal to any fixed direction (section 7.1 gives an expected cosine of about 0.0055 at this size); ours measure -0.0024 and 0.0079 against the gradient.
li2018.does_not_prove: What the full high-dimensional surface looks like; a 2D slice is one view.

ours-model.short: Night School's tiny transformer, the attention lesson's trained weights
ours-model.citation: media/school/attention/model.json, read by tools/school/fill_gradients.mjs (system/school/gradients-landscape.mjs uses the model's own backward pass).
claims: 20,864 numbers; gradient norm of the mean held-out loss on 256 rows: 1.87 at initialisation, 0.124 trained.
A 21 x 21 slice along two filter-normalised random directions on 64 held-out rows: 0.70 at the centre, 13.99 at most; the directions' cosines with the gradient are under 0.01.

An added multiplier s on the readout matrix: the loss is lowest at s = 0.92 (0.6988), against 0.69996 at s = 1; descent from s = 0.05 for 40 steps reaches 0.84 with step 0.05; step 0.2 overshoots to about 2.46 and comes back to 1.27. The 0.92 is measured on 64 held-out rows.
ours-model.n: One trained model; 64 or 256 held-out rows as stated.
ours-model.interval: One seed; no interval across seeds.
ours-model.does_not_prove: Anything about large models' loss surfaces.
